PROJECTS|furwell|tagline: An AI vet app. You describe what is wrong with your pet and it gives you a health report.
PROJECTS|furwell|goal: This was my project for the AIRES competition. [? what was the actual brief — what were you asked to build?] I was the coder on a team of three, with one designer and one researcher. My job was to turn what they gave me into something that actually ran.
PROJECTS|furwell|firstTry: I started with the basics: a Python server that sends the symptoms you type to OpenAI, and gets back a report saying what the condition probably is. Then accounts so you could save your pet. [? what did the designer hand you, and did you build to their design from the start or change it?]
PROJECTS|furwell|wentWrong:
Render puts free servers to sleep, so the first load took about 50 seconds. I fixed that by adding a GitHub Action that pinged my own server every 5 minutes to keep it awake. That is probably what got the service suspended. I had made it worse by trying to make it faster.

The database broke too. psycopg2 would not import on Python 3.13 on Render, so the driver failed and the whole app quietly fell back to saving everything in a data.json file. It looked like it was working and it was not.
PROJECTS|furwell|changed: I turned the pinger off. I pinned psycopg2 to 2.9.10 so it uses a prebuilt wheel and actually imports on 3.13. I also wrote my own rule based moderation for the community posts instead of using a moderation API, because the paid ones cost money.
PROJECTS|furwell|nowDoes: It runs on Render with a Postgres database. You make an account, add your pet, and describe symptoms or upload a photo. It gives you a report with the likely condition, the causes, and a month of meals and exercise. There is a clinic map, a community feed where people post photos and comment, an admin page only I can see, and a paid tier at $7.99 a month. Free accounts get 10 AI checks a day.
PROJECTS|furwell|next: [? what would you fix first if you went back to it?] The whole thing was built in one week for the competition, so there is a lot I would tidy up.
PROJECTS|meatball|tagline: A 4 foot 3 humanoid robot I 3D printed, with two arms that work.
PROJECTS|meatball|goal: [? why a humanoid, and not something easier?] I wanted to build a full sized humanoid with two arms that could actually pick things up, not just a robot arm on a desk.
PROJECTS|meatball|firstTry: I printed two SO-101 arms and mirrored them so one is left and one is right, six joints each. I got the servos from Shenzhen. I do not have leader arms, so instead of a controller I pose one arm with my hands and it records where I put it.
PROJECTS|meatball|wentWrong:
Almost nothing about the hardware stayed still.

The serial ports renumber every time you unplug something, so ACM0 and ACM1 swap and any port I had written down was wrong. Both wrist cameras report the exact same device name, so there is no way to tell them apart from a list. Some of the video devices open perfectly fine and then never send a single frame, because they are not cameras at all.

The worst one was the shoulder. If you hold the arm out at mid range that is where gravity pulls hardest, so the servo is fighting the most there. It does not fail straight away, it just slowly cooks itself while everything looks fine.
PROJECTS|meatball|changed:
I stopped hard coding anything. I wrote a script that takes a snapshot from every camera so I can see which one is which. I worked out the real limit is USB bandwidth, not power, because two raw 640x480 streams at 30fps are about 147 Mbps each.

Then I built a safety layer that everything has to go through. It watches for jams, overheating and slow cooking, it clamps every command so it can never hit the end stop, and it moves around the resting pose instead of mid range so the shoulder is not holding up the whole arm.
PROJECTS|meatball|nowDoes: It is built and standing. Both arms work, six joints each, and I can pose them by hand and play it back. It has a printed head with a face I painted. The safety stack runs on everything.
PROJECTS|meatball|next: I am training LeRobot and SmolVLA policies so the arms learn tasks instead of replaying what I recorded. [? what do you want it to actually do once that works?]
PROJECTS|amongus-ai|tagline: A mod that lets an AI actually play Among Us, in the real game.
PROJECTS|amongus-ai|goal: I wanted to see if an LLM could really play Among Us, not just talk about it. It had to walk around, do tasks, and lie in meetings like a person would.
PROJECTS|amongus-ai|firstTry: Most people do this with screen capture, where the AI looks at a picture of the screen. I read the game's live object state instead, using BepInEx and Reactor. That means I get the actual player positions, tasks, bodies and vents as data, so it is never guessing what it is looking at.
PROJECTS|amongus-ai|wentWrong: The AI is slow. One call takes one to three seconds, and Among Us does not wait for you. If I asked it what to do every frame the game froze, and if I waited for an answer before moving, the bot just stood still and got killed.
PROJECTS|amongus-ai|changed: I split it in two. Sensing runs every tick and is cheap, it just updates what the bot remembers and writes a short text report of what is happening. Thinking runs about every 3 seconds in the background and only sets a high level goal. So the bot keeps moving smoothly while the slow part catches up.
PROJECTS|amongus-ai|nowDoes: It plays. It walks, does tasks, reports bodies, vents and kills, and keeps a memory log of what it saw and when. In meetings it types in chat and votes. [? what happened the first time it played with real people?]
PROJECTS|amongus-ai|next: [? what does it still get obviously wrong?] I only run it in private lobbies with friends, because mods are against the game's terms even in private games.
PROJECTS|void|tagline: A handheld games console I built on an ESP32, with three games on it.
PROJECTS|void|goal: [? what made you build a console instead of just one game?] I wanted a handheld I could load different games onto from a menu, like a tiny Game Boy.
PROJECTS|void|firstTry: [? what was the first version like, and what did it run on?]
PROJECTS|void|wentWrong: Redrawing the whole screen every frame was too slow. [? what did that actually look like when you ran it — flickering, lag, something else?]
PROJECTS|void|changed: In ZombieNights I switched to dirty rectangles, which means only redrawing the parts of the screen that actually changed instead of all of it. Most of the screen is the same from one frame to the next, so there is no point drawing it again.
PROJECTS|void|nowDoes: There is a menu you boot into and three games: ZombieNights, TowerDefense and StickmanQuest. They are separate Arduino sketches and the menu loads them.
PROJECTS|stickman-evolution|tagline: Stick figures that teach themselves to walk, by evolution instead of training.
PROJECTS|stickman-evolution|goal: I wanted creatures that learn to move on their own, without me animating anything or telling them how to walk.
PROJECTS|stickman-evolution|firstTry: Each creature has a small neural network for a brain. I made a population of them with random weights, let them all try to move, kept the ones that got furthest, and mixed those together to make the next generation. No machine learning library, just numpy and a Brain class I wrote.
PROJECTS|stickman-evolution|wentWrong: [? this is the important one — what did the creatures do that you did not expect? evolution almost always finds a stupid shortcut instead of actually learning. what was yours?]
PROJECTS|stickman-evolution|changed: I added a curriculum, so the terrain starts easy and gets harder as the population gets better. Throwing them straight onto hard ground meant everything scored about the same and there was nothing to select for.
PROJECTS|stickman-evolution|nowDoes: It evolves creatures that learn to move over terrain that gets harder. I reused the same engine for a lot of things: a quadruped, a frog, a squid, microgravity, a race arena, 3D terrain, and an FPS agent.
